idiom_name: xs.view.map.filter forced by .to/foldLeft, or Iterator for a single pass
implementation_notes: Scala's collections have the transformer split built in: a View is a collection whose transformations are non-strict - map/filter/flatMap record the operation and return another View, and evaluation happens only when the view is traversed (foreach/foldLeft) or converted with to(...) - so the composition is a value independent of the eventual strict collection type, which is what the 2.13 'view based' redesign made the default implementation strategy. Iterator covers the single-pass and potentially infinite case and LazyList adds memoised element computation, all from the same library. What replaces the classic structure: the view/iterator is the transformation value and the terminal picks the sink (to(List), foldLeft, foreach), so no reducing-function transformer is needed; the literal transducer (a function Reducer => Reducer) is justified when one stack must drive a non-collection sink or be shared with effectful streams.
code_sketch:
val pipeline = (1 to 1_000_000).view            // xs.view: non-strict transformers
  .filter(_ % 2 == 0)
  .map(x => x * x)
  .take(3)                                       // records operations, computes nothing
val out: List[Int] = pipeline.to(List)           // terminal forces it

val infinite = Iterator.iterate(1)(_ + 1).filter(_ % 2 == 0).map(x => x * x)  // single pass
pitfalls: Views recompute on every traversal, and side-effecting transformations inside a view run at a time unrelated to where they are written - the collections guide warns against mixing views with effects.
An Iterator is single-use: consuming it twice yields nothing on the second pass, while a View can be traversed again - choose deliberately and document it.
Operations that need all elements (sorted, groupBy, size) force the view and hang on infinite sources; bound them before forcing.

variants.name: transducers-scala (reducing-function transducers)
variants.implementation_notes: transducers-scala is the literal pattern for Scala: a Transducer[A, B] is a function from a Reducer[B, _] to a Reducer[A, _] (the library documents the rank-2 type), transducers compose with the usual combinators and are applied by operations such as into/run over any reducible source, so one transformation stack can drive a List, an Iterator or a stateful fold. Choose it when the transformation must be reused across contexts the standard library does not unify - particularly where laziness, early termination and non-collection sinks must all hold without adding an effect system. Otherwise View/Iterator covers the same ground with less machinery, better IDE support and no third-party dependency.
pitfalls: The library is not the standard library and has no cats/cats-effect integration: effectful or concurrent streams need fs2, so mixing the two worlds means maintaining two transformation vocabularies.
Rank-2 typing strains inference - a stored Transducer usually needs an explicit type annotation, and error messages are unwieldy when a stage's element type does not line up.
As with every reduction, stateful stages are per-application; reusing a stateful transducer value across runs or threads is a correctness bug, not an optimisation.
